title: Foundational Digital Skills
subtitle: Take control of your phone's settings, use free Google tools for real tasks, keep your device safe and fix everyday problems on your own.
description: A practical, phone-first course for women who use WhatsApp and calls but want to do much more with their smartphone. You will manage data and settings, move information between apps, use Maps, Lens, Keep, Calendar and Sheets for real household and business tasks, protect your phone against loss and theft, and solve common problems yourself. You finish by teaching a skill to another woman and writing your own 90-day plan.
outcomes: Control data, display, sound and updates in your phone's settings and see which apps use your bundle
Move information safely between apps with voice typing, copy and paste, screenshots, Share and the Files app
Use Google Maps, Lens, Keep and Calendar for directions, location sharing, translation, lists and reminders
Build and share a simple Google Sheets record with SUM and COUNTIF, such as an ajo contribution sheet
Secure your phone with a strong lock, Find My Device, backups and a written lost-phone plan
Fix common phone problems with a five-step routine and teach a skill to another person
audience: Women who already make calls and use WhatsApp on an Android smartphone (iPhone users can follow most lessons) and want to use it confidently for family, community and small business tasks.
tools: A smartphone with a Google account (Android preferred; iPhone notes are included where they differ)
Some mobile data or access to Wi-Fi
Free apps: Google Maps, Google (with Lens), Google Keep, Google Calendar, Google Sheets, Files by Google, WhatsApp
A notebook and pen for your self-check, IMEI and plans

modules.title: Know Your Phone and Your Starting Point
modules.overview: You map your digital skills honestly, take control of the settings that cost you money and comfort, and learn the small moves (typing by voice, copying, screenshots, sharing, finding downloads) that every other digital task depends on.

lessons.title: Your digital skills map: five areas and an honest self-check
objectives: Name the five areas of digital skill used in the European DigComp framework
Rate yourself on ten everyday phone tasks using a simple 0 to 2 score
Choose one priority skill for the next three weeks based on a real need
Describe your access situation (own phone, shared phone, data, time) without shame

blocks.text: Many women say "I am not good with phones" when the truth is more specific. You may send voice notes all day but avoid settings. You may pay with a bank app but never have opened a spreadsheet. Digital skill is not one thing. It is a group of skills, and you can be strong in some and new to others. This lesson helps you see exactly where you stand, so the rest of the course works on what you actually need.

blocks.name: mobile-user
blocks.alt: A woman looking at her smartphone screen
blocks.caption: The same phone can do far more once you know which skills you already have and which to build next.

blocks.text: The five areas of digital skill

The European Commission publishes a framework called **DigComp** (the Digital Competence Framework for Citizens). Many training programmes around the world use it because it describes digital skill in plain groups. Its five areas are a useful map for us:

blocks.title: The five DigComp areas
items: Information and data
Communication and collaboration
Creating digital content
Safety
Problem solving
blocks.caption: Every task on your phone falls into one or more of these five areas, so a gap in one area does not mean you are weak in all of them.

head: Area
What it means on your phone
Everyday example
rows: Searching for a bus route, saving a PDF from your child's school
Sending messages, calling, working with others
Voice notes, a video call with your sister, a shared shopping list
Making something new: text, photos, a list, a sheet
A price list photo, a simple record of your ajo contributions
Protecting your phone, accounts, money and privacy
A screen lock, knowing what to do if the phone is stolen
Fixing small problems and learning new tools
Freeing space when the phone says storage is full

blocks.text: The ten-task self-check

Score each task below: **0** means "I cannot do this or I always ask someone", **1** means "I can do it but I am slow or unsure", **2** means "I do it easily on my own". Be honest. Nobody else sees this score, and an honest 0 is more useful than a hopeful 2.

items: Turn mobile data and Wi-Fi on and off, and see how much data each app has used
Make the text on the screen bigger or smaller
Type a message by speaking instead of tapping letters
Copy a phone number or account number from one app and paste it into another
Take a screenshot and send it to someone
Find a file you downloaded yesterday
Find a place on a map and share your location with a family member
Set a reminder that rings on a certain day and time
Lock your phone with a PIN and know how to find it if it is lost
Restart the phone and fix a small problem without help

blocks.text: The highest possible score is 20. The number matters less than the pattern. Look for your zeros. Those are your starting points, and every one of them is taught in this course.

blocks.title: Worked example: reading a self-check score
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi sells foodstuff from a shop in Enugu. She did the self-check on a Sunday evening.
steps: She scored 2 on data, voice notes and screenshots, because she does these every day with customers.
She scored 1 on text size and copying account numbers. She can do them, but slowly.
She scored 0 on finding downloads, reminders, maps, phone security and fixing problems.
Her total was 2 + 2 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 0 = 8 out of 20, but she counted three 2s, two 1s and five 0s.
She asked herself which zero causes her the most trouble. Her answer: she forgets supplier payment days, so reminders came first.
blocks.result: Ngozi chose "set reminders for supplier payments" as her first priority, a specific skill linked to a real cost, instead of the vague goal "get better with my phone".

blocks.text: Your access situation is part of the picture

Skill grows with practice, and practice needs access. Write down three facts: Is the phone yours alone or shared? How much data do you usually have each week? When do you have 15 quiet minutes? If you share a phone, you will need to sign out of accounts and keep a screen lock (Module 3 shows how). If data is tight, practise on Wi-Fi where you can, and choose lessons that work offline first, such as settings and reminders.

blocks.title: You will not break the phone by exploring
blocks.text: Opening Settings, changing text size or turning a switch on and off cannot damage your phone. Almost every setting can be changed back. The real risks are different: sharing your PIN, a one-time password (OTP) or your bank details. Explore freely, but never type those into anything you did not open yourself.

Finally, pick **one priority skill** for this course. A good priority is specific ("find my downloads"), linked to a real need ("I keep losing the school fees PDF") and small enough to practise this week.

takeaways: Digital skill is five areas, not one: information, communication, creating, safety and problem solving
Your zeros on the self-check are your starting points, not a judgement
Access (own or shared phone, data, quiet time) shapes how you practise
A good priority is specific, linked to a real need and small enough for this week

activity.title: Do your ten-task self-check
steps: Copy the ten tasks into a notebook or a note on your phone
Try each task now and score it 0, 1 or 2
Circle every 0 and write next to it one real situation where that skill would have helped you
Write your access facts: own or shared phone, weekly data, best practice time
Write one priority skill in a single sentence
activity.evidence: Your scored self-check with circled zeros and your one-sentence priority (keep it: you will score yourself again at the end).

lessons.title: Phone settings you control: data, display, sound and updates
objectives: Open Quick Settings and the full Settings app and switch Wi-Fi, mobile data and airplane mode
Check which apps use the most data and turn on Data Saver
Adjust text size, brightness and sound so the phone is comfortable to use
Check for system and app updates and explain why they matter

blocks.text: Most of the phone's behaviour is controlled from two places. **Quick Settings** is the panel you get when you swipe down from the top of the screen: it has switches for Wi-Fi, mobile data, torch, airplane mode and brightness. The **Settings app** (the gear icon) holds everything else. On Android phones such as Tecno, Infinix, itel, Samsung and Xiaomi, the menu names differ a little, so if you cannot see an option, tap the magnifying glass at the top of Settings and type its name, for example "data usage".

blocks.name: adjust-settings
blocks.alt: A person adjusting switches and sliders on a large settings panel
blocks.caption: Settings is where you decide how much data, light and sound your phone uses.

blocks.text: Wi-Fi, mobile data and airplane mode

items: **Mobile data** uses your SIM's data bundle. Every megabyte (MB) comes from what you paid for.
**Wi-Fi** uses a wireless network, for example at home, a church office or a workplace. It does not use your bundle.
**Airplane mode** turns off all signals. Turning it on for ten seconds and off again is a quick way to reconnect when the network is stuck.
A **hotspot** shares your mobile data with another phone or laptop. Their usage comes from your bundle.

blocks.text: Find out where your data goes

Open Settings and search for **Data usage** (on many phones: Settings, Network and internet, Data usage or SIM card and mobile data). You will see how much data you used this month and a list of apps from highest to lowest. Video apps (YouTube, TikTok, Facebook video, Instagram Reels) usually sit at the top, because moving pictures carry far more data than text or voice notes.

blocks.title: Worked example: working out where a bundle went
blocks.context: For example, Bisi in Ibadan buys a 3 GB monthly bundle. It ran out after 18 days, and she wanted to know why.
steps: She opened Settings, searched "data usage" and set the period to the current month.
The list showed TikTok 1.8 GB, WhatsApp 0.6 GB, Chrome 0.3 GB and others 0.3 GB, a total of 3.0 GB.
She worked out TikTok's share: 1.8 divided by 3.0 is 0.6, so TikTok used 60 percent of her bundle.
She turned on Data Saver, and in WhatsApp (Settings, Storage and data) set media auto-download on mobile data to "No media".
She decided to watch TikTok mostly on her workplace Wi-Fi.
blocks.result: Bisi found that one app used more than half of her data. Now she knows which single habit to change instead of buying bundles more often.

blocks.text: **Data Saver** (search "Data Saver" in Settings) stops apps in the background from using mobile data. Apps you open still work. Many phones also let you set a **data warning**, so the phone alerts you when you reach an amount you choose, for example 2.5 GB of a 3 GB bundle.
Make the screen and sound work for you

If you squint at the phone or hold it far from your eyes, change it. Search Settings for **Font size** (or Text size) and **Display size**, and move the slider until you read comfortably. **Brightness** affects both comfort and battery: a very bright screen drains the battery faster, and **adaptive brightness** lets the phone adjust to the room. Under **Accessibility** you will also find **TalkBack**, a screen reader that speaks what is on the screen for people with low vision, and **Select to Speak**, which reads chosen text aloud. Under Sound, you can set ringtone, notification and media volume separately, so customers can reach you while your video stays quiet.

blocks.title: Monthly settings check
items: Check data usage per app
Data Saver on if bundle low
Text size comfortable
System update checked
Apps updated in Play Store
blocks.caption: Five quick checks once a month keep your phone cheaper, easier to read and safer.

blocks.text: Updates: why the phone keeps asking

Updates fix security holes and bugs. There are two kinds. **System updates** change Android itself: search Settings for "software update" or "system update". **App updates** come through the Play Store: tap your profile picture, then Manage apps and device, then Updates available. Updates can be large, so run them on Wi-Fi when possible and with the battery above half. A phone that has not been updated for a long time is easier for criminals to attack.

blocks.title: Only update from the real source
blocks.text: Real updates come from Settings or the Play Store. A website pop-up or a WhatsApp message saying "your phone needs an urgent update, download here" is a trick to install harmful software. Close it and check Settings yourself.

On an iPhone, the same ideas apply with different names: Control Centre instead of Quick Settings, Settings, Mobile Data for per-app usage, Display and Brightness for text size, and General, Software Update for updates.

blocks.title: Find what drains your battery
blocks.text: Search Settings for **Battery** and open battery usage. Like data usage, it lists apps from highest to lowest. If one app you rarely open sits near the top, restrict its background activity from that screen or uninstall it. Lowering brightness and shortening the screen timeout (for example to 30 seconds) also help the battery last through a long market day.

takeaways: Swipe down for Quick Settings; use the search bar inside Settings when menu names differ
Data usage shows which apps eat your bundle, and Data Saver limits background use
Text size, brightness and separate volume controls make the phone comfortable
Install updates only from Settings or the Play Store, ideally on Wi-Fi with a good battery

activity.title: Your phone settings audit
steps: Open Data usage and write down your top three apps and how much each used this month
Work out what percentage of your total the top app used
Turn on Data Saver or set a data warning below your bundle size
Adjust font size and brightness until reading is comfortable
Check for a system update and open Updates available in the Play Store
activity.evidence: A note with your top three data apps, the percentage calculation, and a screenshot of your Data Saver or data warning setting.

lessons.title: Moving information between apps: voice typing, copy and paste, screenshots and downloads
objectives: Type a message by voice and correct mistakes before sending
Copy text such as an account number from one app and paste it into another
Take a screenshot and share a photo or file with the Share button
Find downloaded files and open a PDF on your phone

blocks.text: Much of everyday digital work is moving a piece of information from one place to another: an account number from a WhatsApp chat into your bank app, an address into Maps, a receipt into a message. People who do this smoothly are not cleverer. They know five small moves. This lesson teaches all five, and each one saves you from retyping, rewriting by hand or asking someone for help.

blocks.name: share-everywhere
blocks.alt: A person sending content from a phone to several other apps
blocks.caption: Copy, paste and Share let one piece of information travel from app to app without retyping.

blocks.title: Moving information between apps
items: Find the information
Copy or screenshot it
Switch to the other app
Paste or Share
Check before sending
blocks.caption: The same five-step path works for account numbers, addresses, photos and documents.

blocks.text: Move 1: Voice typing

On most Android phones the keyboard is **Gboard** or the phone maker's own keyboard. Tap in any text box, then tap the **microphone** icon on the keyboard and speak. Say "comma", "full stop" or "question mark" to add punctuation. Voice typing is useful when your hands are busy or typing is slow, but it can mishear names and numbers, so always read the text before you press Send. Open the keyboard settings to see which languages it offers.
Move 2: Copy and paste

items: Press and hold on a word until it is highlighted and two small handles appear.
Drag the handles to cover exactly what you need, for example all ten digits of an account number.
Tap **Copy**. The text is now held in the phone's clipboard.
Open the other app, press and hold inside the text box, and tap **Paste**.

blocks.title: Worked example: paying a supplier without typing errors
blocks.context: For example, Halima in Kano receives this WhatsApp message from her fabric supplier: "Pay 45,000 to 0123456789, (bank name), account name Musa Traders." (The numbers here are made up for practice.)
steps: She presses and holds on 0123456789 and adjusts the handles so all ten digits, and nothing else, are selected.
She taps Copy, opens her bank app, chooses Transfer and pastes into the account number box.
The bank app shows the account name. She compares it with the name in the message: Musa Traders. It matches.
She types the amount 45,000 herself, checks the zeros, and completes the transfer.
She takes a screenshot of the success screen and sends it to the supplier.
blocks.result: No digits were mistyped, the account name was confirmed before paying, and both sides have proof of payment. If the name shown by the bank had not matched, Halima would stop and call the supplier on a number she already knows.

blocks.title: Copying is safe; checking is essential
blocks.text: Copying prevents typing mistakes, but it does not prove the number is genuine. Scammers send fake account numbers in messages that look real. Always compare the account name your bank shows, and confirm any new or changed account number by calling the person on a number you saved earlier.
Move 3: Screenshots

On most Android phones, press the **Power** and **Volume down** buttons together for a moment. On many phones you can also swipe down with three fingers or find a Screenshot button in Quick Settings. On iPhones with Face ID, press the **side button** and **Volume up** together. The picture is saved in your Gallery or Photos, usually in a Screenshots album. Before sharing a screenshot, look for private details in the picture, such as your balance or other people's messages, and crop them out with the Edit tool.
Move 4: The Share button

Most apps have a **Share** icon (three dots joined by lines, or a box with an arrow). Tap it on a photo, a PDF, a web page or a location and the phone shows a list of apps: WhatsApp, Gmail, Bluetooth, Nearby Share or Quick Share. This is faster than saving and then attaching, and it keeps the original quality.
Move 5: Finding downloads and opening PDFs

Files you download from a browser or email usually go into a folder called **Download**. Open the **Files** app (on many phones called Files by Google, File Manager or My Files) and tap Downloads. You can sort by date to find the newest. WhatsApp documents can also be found from the chat itself: tap the contact or group name, then Media, links and docs. A **PDF** is a document format that looks the same on every device. Most phones open PDFs in a built-in viewer or in Google Drive. To keep an important PDF safe, rename it with a clear name, such as "School fees invoice Term 1", using the three-dot menu in Files.

Two extra tips make these moves even faster. Gboard keeps a short **clipboard history**: tap the clipboard icon on the keyboard to see recent things you copied and paste an older one, and pin items you use often, such as your business address. Clear it after copying anything private, because other people using your phone could see it. Also, many apps can share text directly: in Maps you can share a place, and in Chrome you can share a page link, so you rarely need to copy long web addresses by hand.

takeaways: Voice typing is fast, but always read names and numbers before sending
Copy and paste prevents typing errors; the account name check prevents paying the wrong person
Power plus Volume down takes a screenshot on most Android phones; crop out private details
Share sends files directly to other apps, and the Files app keeps your downloads

activity.title: The five-moves practice run
steps: Voice type a three-sentence message to yourself (WhatsApp "Message yourself" chat) and correct any mistakes
Copy a phone number from a chat and paste it into the Phone app dialler without calling
Take a screenshot of your home screen, crop it and share it to yourself
Open the Files app, find the newest file in Downloads and rename it clearly
Write down which move was hardest and practise it twice more
activity.evidence: Your "message yourself" chat showing the voice-typed message and cropped screenshot, plus a note naming the hardest move.

quiz.q: Amaka can send voice notes and photos easily but has never set a screen lock and does not know what to do if her phone is stolen. In DigComp terms, which area is her biggest gap?
quiz.explain: Screen locks and a lost-phone plan belong to the Safety area. Her communication skills are already strong, which shows skill is not one single thing.

quiz.q: Which priority goal is best for this course?
options: Set reminders so I stop missing supplier payment days
Become as good as my children
quiz.explain: A good priority is specific, linked to a real need and small enough to practise this week.

quiz.q: Bisi's data usage screen shows YouTube 1.2 GB out of a total of 4 GB used. What share of her data did YouTube use?
quiz.explain: 1.2 divided by 4 is 0.3, which is 30 percent.

quiz.q: A pop-up on a website says "Your phone is infected. Download this update now." What should you do?
options: Download it quickly before the phone gets worse
Forward it to friends as a warning, then download it
Close it and check Settings or the Play Store for real updates
Restart the phone and then download it
quiz.explain: Genuine updates come only from Settings (system) or the Play Store (apps). Pop-ups like this are a common way to install harmful software.

quiz.q: Halima copies an account number from a message and pastes it into her bank app. What is the most important next check?
options: Check that the bank app shows the expected account name before paying
Check that the message has no spelling mistakes
Check that her battery is above 50 percent
Check that the paste used voice typing
quiz.explain: Copying stops typing errors but does not prove the number is genuine. The account name shown by the bank must match the person you intend to pay.

quiz.q: Where will you usually find a PDF you downloaded from a website yesterday?
options: In the Download folder of the Files app
quiz.explain: Browser and email downloads normally go to the Download folder, which you open from the Files app.

modules.title: Everyday Tools That Save Time
modules.overview: You put three free Google tools to real use: Maps and Lens to find places and read the world around you, Keep and Calendar so lists and dates stop slipping, and Sheets to keep a clear, shared record such as an ajo contribution sheet.

lessons.title: Google Maps and Google Lens: find places, share location, read and translate
objectives: Search for a place in Google Maps, get directions and compare travel times
Share your live location for a set time and send a place's plus code
Use Google Lens to copy printed text, translate a label and search what you see
Explain the limits of Maps and Lens results and how to double-check them

blocks.text: Two free apps turn your phone camera and GPS into tools you will use every week. **Google Maps** finds places, shows routes and lets you share where you are. **Google Lens** reads what the camera sees: it can copy printed text, translate a label and search for similar items. Both come installed on most Android phones (Lens is inside the Google app and often in the camera). Both work better with location and camera permission switched on for them only.

blocks.name: location-search
blocks.alt: A woman searching a large map with a location pin
blocks.caption: Maps answers "where is it and how long will it take", and Lens answers "what is this and what does it say".

blocks.text: Google Maps: search, directions and travel time

items: Open Maps and type a place name in the search bar, for example "General Hospital" plus your town.
Tap the result and read the details: address, opening hours if listed, photos and the phone number.
Tap **Directions**. Maps fills in your current location as the start.
Choose the travel mode at the top: car, public transport where available, or walking. Compare the times.
Tap **Start** for turn-by-turn guidance, or simply study the route before you leave.

blocks.text: Travel times are estimates. Traffic, road works and flooding can change them, and in many places public transport details are incomplete. Use Maps as a guide and ask locally when something looks wrong.
Sharing your location safely

In Maps, tap your profile picture, then **Location sharing**, then New share. Choose how long (for example 1 hour) and the person. They can see where you are until the time ends, and you can stop it at any time. This is useful for a long journey or a late return from the market. Share only with people you trust, and check now and again in the same menu who can see your location.

Many homes and shops have no clear street address. Maps gives every spot a **plus code**: a short code of letters and numbers with a plus sign, followed by a town name. Drop a pin by pressing and holding on the map, then tap the pin details to see and copy the plus code. A customer or delivery rider can paste that code into Maps and arrive at the exact gate.

blocks.title: Worked example: helping a delivery rider find a home with no street number
blocks.context: For example, Comfort runs a small cake business from her home in a new estate in Abuja. Riders kept calling her because the street has no signs.
steps: Standing at her gate, she opened Maps, pressed and held on the blue dot to drop a pin.
She tapped the pin details, copied the plus code and also tapped Share to get a Maps link.
She pasted both into a WhatsApp Business quick reply named /location, together with "Blue gate opposite the borehole".
For each order she now sends /location to the rider before he sets out.
blocks.result: The rider's Maps app leads him to her exact gate, and the landmark covers the last few metres. Comfort spends less time on calls during busy baking hours.

blocks.text: Google Lens: let the camera read for you

head: Lens mode
What it does
Example
rows: Finds printed or clear handwritten text in a photo so you can select, copy or listen
Copy the phone number from a poster instead of typing it
Shows the translation over the original text
Read instructions printed in French or Chinese on an imported product
Looks for similar images and pages on the web
Find the name of a fabric pattern or a spare part
Shows explanations for a written question
Help a child understand a maths problem

blocks.text: To use Lens, open the Google app and tap the camera icon in the search bar, or open the camera and look for the Lens icon. Point at the item, then tap the mode you need. In Text mode you can also tap **Listen** on many phones to hear the text read aloud, which helps if the print is small.

blocks.title: Maps or Lens?
items: Google Maps
Google Lens
blocks.caption: Maps works with your location; Lens works with your camera.

blocks.text: Save places you use often

Tap **Save** on any place in Maps to add it to a list such as Favourites or Want to go. You can create your own lists, for example "Suppliers" with the wholesale market, the packaging seller and the bus park for deliveries. Set your **Home** and **Work** addresses under the Saved tab (or in your profile settings) so you can get directions home with one tap. Saved places stay in your Google account and appear again on a new phone after you sign in.

Both apps ask for **permissions**. Maps needs location, and Lens needs the camera. When Android asks, "Allow only while using the app" is usually the best choice: the app works when you open it, but cannot track you in the background. You can change any app's permissions later in Settings, Apps, then the app name, Permissions.

blocks.title: Check before you trust
blocks.text: Lens translations and image matches can be wrong, especially for medicine labels, chemicals and legal papers. For anything about health, safety or money, ask a pharmacist, the seller or a qualified person, and use Lens only to understand the general meaning.

takeaways: Maps gives directions and time estimates; treat times as a guide, not a promise
Location sharing has a time limit you choose; share only with trusted people
A plus code plus a landmark gets visitors to a home with no street address
Lens copies, translates and searches what the camera sees, but check important results

activity.title: Map your world
steps: Search Maps for a place you visit often and compare driving and walking times
Drop a pin at your home or shop and copy its plus code into a note
Share your live location with one trusted person for 15 minutes, then stop the share
Use Lens Text mode to copy a phone number from a printed paper or poster
Use Lens Translate on any label in a language you do not read
activity.evidence: A note containing your plus code and landmark description, plus a screenshot of a Lens translation.

lessons.title: Lists and reminders with Google Keep and Google Calendar
objectives: Create a checklist in Google Keep and share it with another person
Add a time reminder to a note so the phone alerts you
Create a repeating event in Google Calendar with a notification
Decide whether a task belongs in Keep or Calendar

blocks.text: Most of us carry a long list in our heads: the market list, school fees, the day the thrift contribution is due, the customer who promised to pay on Friday. A head is a poor place to store dates. In this lesson you move them into two free tools: **Google Keep** for notes and lists, and **Google Calendar** for things that happen on a date. Both save to your Google account, so they survive if the phone is lost or replaced.

blocks.name: to-do-list
blocks.alt: A woman ticking items on a large to-do list
blocks.caption: Keep holds the list, and Calendar holds the date, so neither has to live in your head.

blocks.text: Google Keep: notes and checklists

items: Install Google Keep from the Play Store if it is not already on your phone, and open it.
Tap the **+** button (or New list). Give the note a title, such as "Saturday market".
Tap the checkbox option to turn it into a checklist, and add items one per line.
At the market, tap each box as you buy. Ticked items move to the bottom.
Tap the bell icon on a note to add a **reminder** for a date and time.
Tap the person icon (Collaborator) to share the note with another Gmail address.

blocks.text: Shared lists update on both phones. If your husband or daughter adds "tomato paste" at home, it appears on your list in the market. You can also give notes colours and **labels** (for example Home, Shop, Church) so they are easy to find, and **pin** the most important note to the top.
Google Calendar: dates that repeat

Calendar is best for anything tied to a day: meetings, payment days, clinic appointments, birthdays. Open Calendar, tap **+**, then Event. Type a title, choose the date and time, and tap **Does not repeat** to change it to weekly, monthly or a custom pattern. Under notifications, choose when the phone should alert you, for example 1 day before and 1 hour before. Two alerts give you time to prepare and a final nudge.

blocks.title: Worked example: never missing a monthly contribution again
blocks.context: For example, Aisha belongs to a women's cooperative in Ilorin that collects ₦10,000 from each member on the last Saturday of every month. She missed two payment days last year and paid a fine each time.
steps: She opened Calendar, tapped + then Event, and typed "Cooperative contribution ₦10,000".
She chose the next last Saturday and set the time to 10:00 am, when meetings start.
She tapped Does not repeat, chose Custom, Monthly, and selected "on the last Saturday".
She set two notifications: 2 days before (to make sure the money is ready) and 1 hour before.
In Keep she made a note "Cooperative" with a checklist for each month and ticks it after paying.
blocks.result: Calendar now alerts her every month without her doing anything more. Over a year she makes 12 payments of ₦10,000, a total of ₦120,000, all on time, and her Keep checklist is a simple record she can show if there is ever a question.

blocks.title: Where does this task belong?
items: Calendar event
Calendar repeating event
Keep checklist
Keep note with reminder
axes: Fixed date or no fixed date
blocks.caption: Fixed dates go in Calendar; lists and loose ideas go in Keep, with a reminder if they need a nudge.

blocks.text: Keep or Calendar? A quick guide

head: Task
Best tool
Why
rows: Many items, no fixed time, easy to tick
A fixed date that needs an alert
No date, just ideas to keep
Call a customer back on Friday
Keep note with reminder or Calendar
Either works; pick one and be consistent

blocks.title: Make alerts reach you
blocks.text: If reminders never ring, check Settings, Apps, Keep or Calendar, Notifications, and make sure notifications are allowed. Some phones also put apps to sleep to save battery; search Settings for "battery optimisation" and set Calendar and Keep to not be restricted.
A two-minute daily habit

items: Each morning, open Calendar and look at today and tomorrow. Nothing should surprise you.
Open Keep and read your pinned notes. Tick off anything already done.
Add anything new that came up yesterday: a promise, a payment, a phone call to return.
Each Sunday, look one week ahead in Calendar and prepare money or materials for fixed dates.

blocks.text: If you share a phone with family members, Keep and Calendar still work, but they are tied to whichever Google account is signed in. Agree on one account for shared family lists, and keep your personal or business reminders on your own account where possible. Anyone using the phone can see notes and events, so do not store PINs, passwords or bank details in Keep, even in a note you think is private.
Start small. Move just three things out of your head this week: one list, one fixed date and one repeating date. When those work, add more.

takeaways: Keep is for lists and notes; Calendar is for anything tied to a date
Shared Keep lists update on every collaborator's phone
Repeating Calendar events with two notifications stop missed payment days
If alerts do not ring, check app notifications and battery optimisation

activity.title: Three things out of your head
steps: Create a Keep checklist for your next market trip with at least six items
Share the list with one family member or colleague and ask them to add an item
Create a Calendar event for one fixed date coming up, with a notification
Create one repeating Calendar event (weekly or monthly) with two notifications
Check that notifications are allowed for both apps
activity.evidence: Screenshots of the shared Keep list (showing the added item) and the repeating Calendar event settings.

lessons.title: Your first spreadsheet: an ajo contribution record in Google Sheets
objectives: Create a Google Sheet on your phone and enter data in rows and columns
Use SUM and COUNTIF formulas to total payments and count missed ones
Freeze the header row and format money columns
Share the sheet with view-only access so others can check without changing it

blocks.text: A **spreadsheet** is a grid of boxes called **cells**. Columns run down and are named with letters (A, B, C). Rows run across and are numbered (1, 2, 3). Each cell has an address made of its column and row, for example **B2**. The power of a spreadsheet is that it can add, count and check numbers for you, so the totals are always right even when you change one entry. **Google Sheets** is free, works on a phone and saves automatically to your Google account.

blocks.name: spreadsheets
blocks.alt: A woman working with a large spreadsheet of rows and columns
blocks.caption: A simple sheet with names, weeks and totals replaces a notebook that only one person can read.

blocks.text: The record we will build

An **ajo** (also called esusu or adashi in different places) is a rotating savings group. Each member pays the same amount on a set day, and each week one member collects the whole amount. Records are often kept in one person's notebook, which leads to arguments when a page is lost or a payment is forgotten. A shared sheet solves this.

blocks.title: Worked example: an eight-member weekly ajo
blocks.context: For example, Funmi coordinates an ajo of 8 market women in Abeokuta. Each pays ₦5,000 every Monday, and one member collects each week.
steps: Weekly pot: 8 members × ₦5,000 = ₦40,000 collected by one member each week.
The cycle lasts 8 weeks, so every member collects once. Each pays 8 × ₦5,000 = ₦40,000 in total and receives ₦40,000 once.
In Sheets, Funmi types "Member" in A1 and "Week 1" to "Week 8" in B1 to I1. Members' names go in A2 to A9.
Each Monday she types 5000 next to each member who has paid and 0 for anyone who has not.
In A10 she types "Total" and in B10 she types =SUM(B2:B9). If all paid, it shows 40000.
In A11 she types "Missed" and in B11 she types =COUNTIF(B2:B9,0). It counts the zeros in that week.
blocks.result: In Week 3, one member had not paid. B10 showed 35000 instead of 40000 and B11 showed 1, so Funmi knew at a glance that the collector was ₦5,000 short and exactly who to follow up with.

blocks.title: Building the ajo sheet
items: Header row: Member, Week 1-8
Names in column A
5000 or 0 each week
SUM row for totals
COUNTIF row for missed
Share as viewer
blocks.caption: Build the structure once, then each week you only type the payments.

blocks.text: Step by step on your phone

items: Install Google Sheets from the Play Store, open it and tap **+** then New spreadsheet.
Tap the file name at the top left and rename it, for example "Ajo Cycle 1 2026".
Double tap a cell to type in it. Type the headers in row 1 and the names in column A.
Every formula starts with an equals sign. Type =SUM(B2:B9) in B10. The colon means "from B2 to B9".
To copy the formula to the other weeks, tap B10, tap Copy, select C10 to I10, then Paste. Sheets adjusts the letters for each column automatically.
Select row 1, open the format or row menu and choose **Freeze** so the headers stay visible as you scroll.
Select the money cells, tap the format (A) icon, then Cell, Number format, and choose a number format with thousands separators.

blocks.text: Sharing without losing control

Tap the three-dot menu, then **Share and export**, then Share. Add members' Gmail addresses and choose **Viewer**. Viewers can see the sheet but cannot change it. Keep **Editor** access for yourself and perhaps one trusted assistant. Sheets also keeps a **version history** (in the web version, File, Version history), which shows who changed what and when, so mistakes can be traced and undone.

blocks.title: Keep personal details out of shared sheets
blocks.text: Do not put members' bank account numbers, BVN, NIN, home addresses or phone PINs in a shared sheet. Names and amounts are enough for an ajo record. If a link is ever set to "Anyone with the link", anyone who gets that link can open the sheet, so prefer adding named people.

Once you are comfortable, the same pattern works for a customer debt list, a stock count or a family budget: headers across the top, one row per item, SUM for totals and COUNTIF to count something you care about.
Common beginner mistakes and how to fix them

items: **Typing ₦ or commas into number cells.** Type 5000, not ₦5,000. Use number format to show commas, otherwise SUM may ignore the cell.
**Forgetting the equals sign.** SUM(B2:B9) without = is just text. Every formula starts with =.
**Leaving a cell empty instead of 0.** COUNTIF(B2:B9,0) counts zeros, not empty cells, so type 0 for a missed payment.
**Wrong range.** If you add a ninth member in row 10, update the formulas to B2:B10 and move the Total row down.
**Editing on a bad connection.** Sheets saves changes when you are back online, but wait for the saved message before closing the app.

takeaways: Cells have addresses such as B2; formulas start with an equals sign
=SUM(B2:B9) totals a range; =COUNTIF(B2:B9,0) counts how many cells equal zero
Freeze the header row and use number formats for money
Share as Viewer, keep Editor access small, and never store account numbers or IDs in the sheet

activity.title: Build a real record
steps: Create a new Google Sheet for a real group, business or family record (ajo, debts owed to you, or weekly sales)
Enter at least five rows of names or items and at least four columns of amounts
Add a SUM row and a COUNTIF row and check the totals by hand once
Freeze the header row and format the money cells
Share it as Viewer with one person and ask them to confirm they can see it
activity.evidence: A screenshot of your sheet showing the formulas working, and a note of your hand-check calculation matching the SUM.

quiz.q: A customer cannot find Comfort's house because the street has no name sign. What is the best thing to send?
options: A Maps plus code or pin link plus a nearby landmark
The name of the nearest city
quiz.explain: A plus code or pin link leads Maps to the exact spot, and a landmark helps with the last few metres.

quiz.q: Halima wants to read assembly instructions printed in French on an imported mixer. Which tool helps most?
quiz.explain: Lens Translate reads printed text through the camera and shows the translation on top of it.

quiz.q: Which task belongs in Google Calendar rather than a Keep checklist?
options: A list of 12 items to buy at the market
Clinic appointment on the first Tuesday of every month
quiz.explain: Anything tied to a date, especially a repeating one, belongs in Calendar with notifications.

quiz.q: An ajo has 6 members paying ₦4,000 each week. How much does the collector receive each week?
In Funmi's sheet, B10 shows =SUM(B2:B9) as 35000 instead of 40000. What does this most likely mean?
options: One member paid 0 that week, so the pot is ₦5,000 short
Sheets cannot add numbers on a phone
quiz.explain: With 8 members at ₦5,000, a full week totals 40000. A total of 35000 means ₦5,000 is missing, and the COUNTIF row would show 1 missed payment.

quiz.q: Funmi wants members to see the ajo sheet but not change it. Which access should she give?
options: Anyone with the link as Editor
quiz.explain: Viewer access lets people see the sheet without editing, while Funmi keeps control as the editor.

modules.title: Staying in Control and Sharing Your Skills
modules.overview: You protect the phone itself and prepare for loss or theft, learn a calm routine for fixing common problems without help, and then pass a skill on to another woman while proving your own progress with a skills log and a 90-day plan.

lessons.title: Protect the phone itself: screen lock, Find My Device, backups and a lost-phone plan
objectives: Set a strong screen lock and hide sensitive content on the lock screen
Turn on Find My Device and know how to locate, lock or erase a lost phone
Back up contacts, photos and WhatsApp chats to your Google account
Write a one-page lost-phone plan with IMEI and emergency numbers

blocks.text: Your phone now holds your contacts, photos, bank app, WhatsApp chats and perhaps business records. If it is stolen or dropped in water, two questions matter: can a stranger get into it, and can you get your information back? This lesson answers both. It focuses on the device itself. Passwords and two-step verification for online accounts are covered in the WODDI course Internet Basics and Online Safety.

blocks.name: mobile-encryption
blocks.alt: A phone with a padlock symbol protecting its contents
blocks.caption: A screen lock and a backup mean a lost phone is an inconvenience, not a disaster.

blocks.text: Step 1: A real screen lock

Open Settings and search **Screen lock**. Choose a **PIN** of at least 6 digits or a password. Avoid 123456, 000000, your birth year or your phone number, because these are the first things a thief tries. Pattern locks are weaker, because the smudge on the screen and people watching over your shoulder can reveal them. You can add **fingerprint** or face unlock for convenience, but the PIN remains the backup. Then search **Lock screen notifications** and choose to hide sensitive content, so bank alerts and one-time passwords (OTPs) do not appear on a locked screen.
Step 2: Find My Device

Google's **Find My Device** lets you locate an Android phone from another phone or a computer. Search Settings for "Find My Device" and make sure it is on, and keep Location on. If the phone goes missing, go to **google.com/android/find** on any browser (or the Find My Device app on a friend's phone), sign in with your Google account and you can: see the phone's last location on a map, make it **ring** at full volume even on silent, **lock** it with a message and a contact number, or **erase** it if you believe it is gone for good. Erasing removes your data, so locate and lock first. The phone must be switched on and connected for these to work immediately. iPhones have a similar service called Find My.
Step 3: Backups

items: **Contacts:** save new contacts to your Google account, not to the SIM or "phone only". In the Contacts app, check the account shown when you save.
**Photos:** in Google Photos, turn on Backup. Choose "backup over Wi-Fi only" if data is costly. The free Google account storage is shared across Gmail, Drive and Photos.
**WhatsApp:** in WhatsApp, Settings, Chats, Chat backup, link your Google account and choose how often to back up.
**Phone settings and apps:** search Settings for "Backup" and turn on backup to your Google account.

blocks.text: Step 4: Your lost-phone plan

Dial *#06# on your phone, exactly as written. The screen shows your **IMEI**, a 15-digit number that identifies the handset itself (dual-SIM phones show two). Write it on paper with your phone make and model and keep it at home, not in the phone case. The network and the police can use it when you report a theft.

blocks.title: First hour after losing your phone
items: Ring it from Find My Device
Lock it with a message
Call bank to block mobile banking
Ask network to block SIM
Change Google password
Report with IMEI
blocks.caption: Acting in this order protects your money first, then your accounts, then gives you a record for recovery.

blocks.title: Worked example: a phone lost in a bus
blocks.context: For example, Grace left her phone on a bus in Port Harcourt at 6:30 pm. She had set up Find My Device and kept her IMEI in a notebook at home.
steps: At 6:45 pm, on her sister's phone, she opened google.com/android/find and signed in. The map showed the phone moving along the bus route.
She tapped Secure device and added the message "This phone is lost. Please call my sister" together with her sister's number.
She called her bank's helpline (the number printed on the back of her debit card) and asked them to block mobile banking on the lost device.
She called her network's customer care to block the SIM and asked how to get a SIM replacement with the same number.
Next morning the bus driver called the number on the lock screen and she collected her phone at the park.
blocks.result: Because the phone was locked within 15 minutes and the bank was alerted, nobody could open her apps or move her money. Her contacts and photos were also safe in her Google backup, so even if the phone had not come back, she would have lost the device, not her information.

blocks.text: If you share a phone with family members, you can still protect yourself. Keep a screen lock that only adults in the home know, sign out of banking apps after each use, and turn off "save password" prompts in the browser for bank websites. On many Android phones you can also add a **guest** or second user profile (search Settings for "Multiple users"), so children use their own space without seeing your messages or apps.

blocks.title: Get numbers from a trusted source
blocks.text: When a phone is lost, scammers sometimes call pretending to be the bank or the person who found it, and ask for OTPs or PINs. Use only the helpline printed on your card, on your bank's official app or website, or given at the bank branch, and never share an OTP or PIN with anyone who calls you.

takeaways: Use a 6-digit PIN or password, not a birthday or a pattern, and hide sensitive lock-screen content
Find My Device can ring, lock or erase a lost Android phone from any browser
Back up contacts, photos and WhatsApp to your Google account before anything goes wrong
Keep your IMEI (dial *#06#) and a lost-phone plan on paper at home

activity.title: Secure and back up your phone
steps: Set or strengthen your screen lock and hide sensitive lock-screen notifications
Check that Find My Device and Location are on, then test it from another device by making your phone ring
Turn on Google Photos backup and WhatsApp chat backup
Dial *#06# and write your IMEI, phone model, bank helpline and network helpline on paper
Keep the paper in a safe place at home
activity.evidence: A photo of your written lost-phone plan with the IMEI digits partly covered, and a screenshot of WhatsApp chat backup settings.

lessons.title: Fixing common phone problems yourself: a five-step troubleshooting routine
objectives: Follow a five-step routine to fix most everyday phone problems
Free up storage space safely using the Files app and app storage settings
Fix connection problems with airplane mode and data checks
Search for help using the exact error message and judge whether a source is trustworthy

blocks.text: Phones misbehave: WhatsApp will not send, the screen freezes, an app closes by itself, or the phone says storage is full. Many people hand the phone to a child or a repair stand at once. Most of these problems have the same few causes, and you can fix them with a calm routine. Problem solving is one of the five DigComp areas, and it is the skill that makes every other skill last, because apps will keep changing.

blocks.name: fixing-bugs
blocks.alt: A person working through a problem on a large screen with tools
blocks.caption: A simple routine fixes most problems before you need a repair stand.

blocks.title: Five-step troubleshooting routine
items: Describe the problem exactly
Check connection and battery
Close app, then restart phone
Check storage and updates
Search the exact message
blocks.caption: Go in order: the early steps are quick and fix the most problems.

blocks.text: Step 1: Describe the problem exactly

"My phone is not working" cannot be fixed. "WhatsApp messages show one grey tick and do not deliver since this morning" can. Write down what happens, when it started, which app, and any message on the screen. Take a screenshot of the error. This also helps if you later ask someone for help.
Step 2: Check connection and battery

items: Is mobile data or Wi-Fi switched on in Quick Settings? Is there signal?
Is your bundle finished? Check with your network's balance code or app.
Turn **airplane mode** on for ten seconds, then off. This forces the phone to reconnect.
Is Battery Saver on? It can stop apps from refreshing in the background.
Open a website in Chrome. If it does not load either, the problem is the connection, not the app.

blocks.text: Step 3: Close the app, then restart

Open the recent apps view (swipe up and hold, or tap the square button) and swipe the problem app away. Open it again. If that fails, **restart** the phone: hold the Power button (on some phones Power and Volume up) and choose Restart. A restart clears temporary memory and solves a surprising number of freezes. If the screen is frozen and will not respond, holding the Power button for about 10 to 20 seconds forces most Android phones to restart.
Step 4: Check storage and updates

When storage is nearly full, apps crash and photos will not save. Open Settings and search **Storage** to see what is using space. The **Files by Google** app has a Clean tab that suggests junk files, duplicate files and large videos to remove. WhatsApp is often the biggest user: in WhatsApp, Settings, Storage and data, Manage storage, you can see large files and forwarded videos and delete them in bulk. You can also open Settings, Apps, choose an app, Storage, and tap **Clear cache**. Clearing cache removes temporary files and is safe. **Clear data** (or Clear storage) is different: it resets the app and can delete your saved information, so avoid it unless you have a backup. Finally, check for app and system updates as in Module 1.

blocks.title: Worked example: "Storage full" before a family event
blocks.context: For example, Chiamaka in Owerri could not take photos at her niece's naming ceremony. The phone said storage was full: 30.6 GB used of 32 GB, leaving only 1.4 GB.
steps: She opened WhatsApp, Settings, Storage and data, Manage storage, and sorted by size. Forwarded videos in three groups used 4.2 GB. She deleted them.
In Files by Google, Clean, she removed 0.9 GB of junk files and 1.1 GB of duplicate images.
She had already turned on Google Photos backup, so she used Free up space to remove 3.5 GB of photos that were safely backed up.
New free space: 1.4 + 9.7 = 11.1 GB.
blocks.result: In about 15 minutes Chiamaka went from 1.4 GB to 11.1 GB free without losing anything important, and the camera worked again. She now checks WhatsApp storage once a month.

blocks.text: Step 5: Search the exact message

If the problem remains, type the **exact error message** in Google, plus your phone model, for example "Tecno Spark 10 app keeps stopping". Prefer answers from the official help sites (support.google.com, the phone maker's site, faq.whatsapp.com) or trusted tutorial sites such as GCFGlobal. Be careful with any site or video that asks you to install an unknown "cleaner" app, enter your Google password or pay to fix a simple problem.

blocks.title: When to stop and get a qualified repairer
blocks.text: Stop using the phone and take it to a trusted repairer if the battery is swollen, the phone gets very hot, smells of burning, or has been in water. Do not charge a swollen or water-damaged phone. Before handing any phone in for repair, back it up and, where possible, sign out of banking apps.

takeaways: Describe the problem exactly and screenshot any error before you start
Connection checks and a restart fix many problems in under two minutes
Clear cache is safe; Clear data can delete information, so back up first
Search the exact error with your phone model and trust official help sites
Swollen, very hot or water-damaged phones need a qualified repairer, not home fixes

activity.title: Your storage clean-up and problem log
steps: Write down your phone's used and free storage from Settings, Storage
Clean WhatsApp storage and run Files by Google Clean (back up first)
Write down the new free storage and calculate how much you freed
Start a problem log: date, problem, steps tried, what fixed it
Next time something goes wrong, follow the five steps and log it
activity.evidence: Before and after storage screenshots with your calculation, and the first entry in your problem log.

lessons.title: Teaching another woman, proving your progress and your 90-day plan
objectives: Teach one digital skill to another person using the I do, We do, You do method
Re-score the ten-task self-check and compare it with your starting score
Document one tool you now use for a real purpose
Write a 90-day plan with one next skill, weekly practice and one person to teach

blocks.text: You have built real skills in this course: settings, the five moves, Maps and Lens, Keep and Calendar, a spreadsheet, phone security and troubleshooting. Two things make these skills stick. The first is teaching someone else, because explaining a skill shows you where your own understanding is solid. The second is measuring your progress, so you can see how far you have come and choose the next step on purpose.

blocks.name: teaching
blocks.alt: A woman teaching another person in front of a board
blocks.caption: Teaching one skill to one woman spreads confidence further than any course can alone.

blocks.text: How to teach a phone skill: I do, We do, You do

Teachers widely use a simple three-stage method called gradual release. It works very well for phone skills, because the most common mistake is the helper taking the phone and doing everything quickly while the learner watches.

blocks.title: I do, We do, You do
items: I do: show slowly once
We do: she taps, you guide
You do: she does it alone
Check: she explains it back
blocks.caption: Repeat the cycle until she can do the task alone and explain it in her own words.

items: **Use her phone, not yours.** Menus differ between brands. She needs to learn on the phone she will use.
**Keep your hands off.** After your one demonstration, she taps every time. Point and describe instead: "the gear icon at the top right".
**One skill per session.** Fifteen minutes on one skill beats an hour on ten.
**Name the words.** Say "Settings", "Share", "screenshot" so she can search for them later.
**Never ask for her PIN or passwords.** Ask her to unlock the phone herself and to type private details while you look away.

blocks.title: Worked example: teaching a neighbour to set a reminder
blocks.context: For example, Kemi taught her neighbour Mama Tunde, a pepper seller in Osogbo who often forgot her monthly thrift contribution day.
steps: I do: Kemi asked Mama Tunde to unlock her own phone, then slowly showed once how to open Calendar, tap +, type "Thrift contribution" and set the date, saying each step aloud.
We do: she deleted the event and Mama Tunde made it again, tapping every button while Kemi pointed and named each item.
You do: Kemi stepped back. Mama Tunde made a second event, "Buy pepper stock", on her own. She got stuck at Repeat, so Kemi only pointed to the words Does not repeat.
Check: Mama Tunde explained the steps back in Yoruba in her own words.
Kemi wrote in her skills log: date, person, skill, about 20 minutes, she can now do it alone.
blocks.result: Mama Tunde now sets her own reminders, and Kemi has evidence of sharing a skill for her capstone. Kemi also noticed she had to think about where the Repeat option was, which showed her one step to practise herself.

blocks.text: When your learner gets stuck

items: **She forgets a step:** let her try to find it first. Ask "What do you see on the screen?" before you point.
**Her phone looks different from yours:** use the search bar inside Settings together and read the menu names aloud.
**She is afraid of pressing the wrong thing:** show her the Back button and explain that most taps can be undone.
**She is tired or upset:** stop and agree on a short session another day. Confidence builds faster with short, happy sessions.
**You do not know the answer:** search it together using the exact words on the screen. This teaches her problem solving too.

blocks.text: Measure your progress
Go back to the ten-task self-check from Module 1. Score each task again 0, 1 or 2 and compare. Then complete a simple **skills log**, a table you keep in Keep, Sheets or a notebook.

head: Date
Skill
Can do alone now?
Real use
Evidence
rows: Ajo sheet with SUM and COUNTIF

blocks.text: The real test of a digital skill is whether it changed something in your life: less data wasted, no missed payment, fewer arguments over records, a lost phone recovered. Write that down for at least one tool. This is the "one productivity tool you have adopted" part of your capstone.
Your 90-day plan

A good 90-day plan has four parts: **one next skill** (for example online payments safety, Canva for price lists, or WhatsApp Business), **a weekly practice slot** (day, time, 15 to 30 minutes), **one person to teach** each month, and **a check date** at day 30, 60 and 90 when you re-score yourself. Free, well-made lessons on many phone and Google skills are available at GCFGlobal (edu.gcfglobal.org), and other WODDI Institute courses build directly on this one.

blocks.title: Keep it small and real
blocks.text: One skill done well in 90 days, used for a real purpose and taught to three women, is worth more than a long list of skills you meant to learn. Small, repeated practice is what builds confidence.

takeaways: Teach with I do, We do, You do on her phone, with your hands off
Never ask for another person's PIN or passwords while helping
Re-score the self-check and keep a skills log with real-use evidence
A 90-day plan needs one next skill, a weekly slot, someone to teach and check dates

activity.title: Teach, measure and plan
steps: Teach one skill from this course to one person using I do, We do, You do
Record the session in your skills log: date, person, skill, time and result
Re-score the ten-task self-check and write your old and new scores side by side
Write your 90-day plan with all four parts
Put your three check dates (day 30, 60, 90) in Google Calendar
activity.evidence: Your skills log with the teaching entry, both self-check scores, and your written 90-day plan with check dates.

quiz.q: Which screen lock gives the best protection?
options: Pattern lock shaped like the letter L
A 6-digit PIN that is not a birthday, phone number or simple sequence
No lock, but hide the phone well
quiz.explain: A 6-digit PIN that is not easy to guess is strong. Simple sequences, birth years and patterns are the first things thieves try or can see.

quiz.q: Grace's phone is lost but still switched on. What should she do first?
options: Use Find My Device to ring it and lock it with a contact message
Post on Facebook that it is lost
quiz.explain: Locate and lock first. Erasing removes the data and stops her from tracking it, so it is the last option.

quiz.q: WhatsApp will not send messages and Chrome will not load any website either. What is the most likely cause?
quiz.explain: If several apps cannot reach the internet, the problem is the connection. Check data, signal and bundle, and toggle airplane mode.

quiz.q: Chiamaka has 2.1 GB free. She frees 3.0 GB from WhatsApp and 1.4 GB from junk files. How much free space does she have now?
Which storage action can delete an app's saved information?
quiz.explain: Clear data resets the app and can delete saved information. Clear cache only removes temporary files.

quiz.q: Kemi is teaching her neighbour to set a reminder. What is the best approach?
options: Take the phone and set it up quickly for her
Show once, then let her tap each step on her own phone while Kemi guides
Send her a long text explaining everything
Ask for her PIN so Kemi can practise later
quiz.explain: I do, We do, You do on the learner's own phone builds real skill. Never ask for someone's PIN.

finalQuiz.q: Ngozi scored 0 on reminders, maps and phone security but 2 on voice notes. What does this tell her?
options: She is bad with phones in general
Her skills are strong in communication but she has specific gaps to work on
She should stop using voice notes
finalQuiz.explain: Digital skill is several areas. Her zeros show exactly where to start, while her communication skills are already strong.

finalQuiz.q: Bisi's 2 GB bundle keeps running out. What is the most useful first step?
options: Check Data usage to see which apps use the most
Turn the phone off at night
finalQuiz.explain: Data usage shows which apps eat the bundle, so she can change the one habit that matters.

finalQuiz.q: Which way of receiving an update is safe?
options: A link in a WhatsApp message saying update urgently
A website pop-up warning of a virus
Settings, Software update, or Updates available in the Play Store
A file sent by Bluetooth from a stranger
finalQuiz.explain: Real system and app updates come only from Settings and the Play Store.

finalQuiz.q: Halima copies an account number into her bank app and the bank shows a different account name from the one in the message. What should she do?
options: Pay anyway because she copied it exactly
Stop and call the supplier on a number she already has saved
Change the name in the message
Send half the money to test
finalQuiz.explain: A mismatched name is a warning sign of a wrong or fake account. Confirm through a channel she already trusts.

finalQuiz.q: How do you take a screenshot on most Android phones?
options: Press Power and Volume down together
Hold the Home button for 30 seconds
finalQuiz.explain: Power plus Volume down is the standard Android screenshot shortcut; many phones also offer a three-finger swipe or a Quick Settings button.

finalQuiz.q: Comfort's customers cannot find her house. Which Maps feature helps most?
options: A plus code or dropped pin link with a landmark
Street View of the city centre
finalQuiz.explain: A plus code identifies the exact spot even without a street address, and a landmark helps at the gate.

finalQuiz.q: Which task fits Google Keep best?
options: A shared shopping list that family members add to
A fixed meeting next Tuesday at 4 pm
finalQuiz.explain: Keep is ideal for lists and notes, especially shared ones. Fixed dates belong in Calendar.

finalQuiz.q: A savings group has 10 members paying ₦3,000 every week. What is the weekly pot, and how long is a full cycle so everyone collects once?
finalQuiz.explain: 10 × ₦3,000 = ₦30,000 each week, and with 10 members a full cycle takes 10 weeks.

finalQuiz.q: In Google Sheets, what does =COUNTIF(B2:B9,0) do?
options: Adds all numbers from B2 to B9
Counts how many cells from B2 to B9 contain 0
finalQuiz.explain: COUNTIF counts cells in a range that meet a condition, here cells equal to 0, which shows missed payments.

finalQuiz.q: Grace wants to be able to report her phone if it is stolen. What should she write down now and keep at home?
options: Her IMEI from *#06#, phone model and helpline numbers
finalQuiz.explain: The IMEI identifies the handset for the network and police reports. PINs and passwords should never be written alongside it.

finalQuiz.q: A phone's battery has swollen and the back cover is lifting. What should the owner do?
options: Press the cover back and keep charging
Stop using and charging it, and take it to a qualified repairer
Put it in the fridge to cool
finalQuiz.explain: A swollen battery is a fire risk. Stop using and charging it and get qualified help.

options: Learn everything about technology by December
Learn WhatsApp Business: practise Wednesdays 8 pm for 20 minutes, teach one woman each month, re-score on days 30, 60 and 90
Watch videos when I have time
Ask my children to handle my phone
finalQuiz.explain: A strong plan names one skill, a regular practice slot, someone to teach and check dates.

capstone.title: Digital Confidence Project
capstone.brief: A short portfolio (in Google Keep, Google Docs, a notebook or a WhatsApp "message yourself" chat) that proves what you can now do: your before and after self-check, one tool you have adopted for a real purpose with evidence of the result, one skill you taught to another person, and a 90-day plan.
steps: Put your Module 1 self-check score and your new score side by side, and list every task that moved from 0 or 1 to 2
Choose one tool you now use for a real purpose (for example a shared Keep list, a repeating Calendar reminder or an ajo sheet in Google Sheets) and write what it changed, with a screenshot
Show one safety step you completed: your screen lock and Find My Device test, or your written lost-phone plan with the IMEI partly covered
Record one teaching session using I do, We do, You do: who, which skill, how long and the result
Write your 90-day plan: one next skill, a weekly practice slot, one person to teach each month and check dates at day 30, 60 and 90
Share the portfolio with your WODDI cohort lead or study group if your programme asks for it, removing any private numbers first
evidence: Before and after ten-task self-check scores
Screenshot and short note on one productivity tool in real use
Proof of one device safety step (screen lock, Find My Device test or lost-phone plan)
Skills log entry for one teaching session
Written 90-day plan with check dates in Calendar
No PINs, passwords, account numbers or ID numbers anywhere in the portfolio
